items.feedback: Right. What makes a system an agent is the loop: the model picks an action, the program runs it, and the result comes back. A longer prompt or a bigger model only changes what a single call can do.

You picked 'it reads the calendar by opening the booking system on its own'. That is tempting because the whole thing feels like one smart assistant. But the model only outputs text. Here that text is a request naming check_calendar with the laser cutter and tomorrow's date as arguments (option c). The program around the model runs the tool and sends the result back. Think of the model as writing an order slip and the program as the person who fetches the item.

Right. The agent repeats the same failing step, so more steps or more context add nothing. A step limit is a stopping condition that ends the loop and hands the problem back to a person. Every agent you build needs one, and it also caps your cost.

The answer is 4, not 1. You wrote that the model 'runs the 3 tools itself', which is the same idea as in q2. The model is called once per input it receives: the question, then each of the three tool results. The first three calls each end in one tool request, and the fourth writes the final answer. The program runs the tools between calls, and those runs are not model calls. This also matters for your budget: each call costs money, so a four-step request costs about four calls.

'It sends it back to the model' is the right half: that is what happens. You left out why. The program adds the result to the model's next input and calls the model again so the model can use it to decide its next step or write the final answer. Next time, add the 'so that...' part.

The first half is right: the model is sent a list of tools, each with a name and a description, and picks the one that fits. The second half is wrong. The model does not remember earlier sessions on its own. Each call starts fresh with only what the program puts in its input, so any memory between sessions has to be saved and added back by the program. This is the topic coming up next.

summary: You have the shape of the loop: what makes a system an agent, why it needs a stopping condition, and that the model chooses tools from their descriptions. Two things to fix. First, the model only outputs text; the program runs the tools and calls the model again after each result (you missed q2 and q4 on this, and it decides the call count and cost). Second, the model has no memory of its own between sessions. Next step: re-trace your laser cutter request on paper, writing 'model output' or 'program action' beside every step, and count the model calls.
